note: Discovery leads for topic workers. Every topic must still research and verify its own sources; nothing here is pre-approved for reuse. A broad history survey (historiography/skills + world history + U.S. history). Accuracy of dates/sequence/attribution and even-handed, multi-perspective treatment are the defining controls.

tierA.provider: OpenStax — World History (vol. 1 & 2) and U.S. History
tierA.useFor: authoritative CC BY OER survey text for world and U.S. history — definitions, narrative, dates

tierA.provider: U.S. Library of Congress & National Archives (NARA)
tierA.useFor: primary sources, founding documents, and teaching-with-sources guidance (public domain)

tierA.provider: Stanford History Education Group (SHEG) / Reading Like a Historian
tierA.useFor: historical-thinking concepts (sourcing, contextualization, corroboration, close reading)

tierB.useFor: peer-reviewed encyclopedia entries on events, places, and people — REFERENCE_ONLY, verify dates
primary-source texts (treaties, documents) — public domain / REFERENCE_ONLY
world heritage, archaeology, and cultural history — REFERENCE_ONLY
REFERENCE_ONLY cross-check of dates and definitions; never the sole source for a claim

cautions: ACCURACY IS A PRIMARY CONTROL. Verify every DATE, sequence, name, and attribution against an authoritative source before publishing. Do not state a contested or approximate date as exact — give ranges (e.g. 'c. 3100 BCE') where scholarship does. A wrong date or a garbled name is a blocking defect.

EVEN-HANDED, MULTI-PERSPECTIVE treatment is the second primary control. History is interpretive: distinguish established FACTS (what happened, when) from INTERPRETATION (why, and what it meant), and where historians genuinely disagree, present the major perspectives without declaring one correct. Avoid nationalism, triumphalism, and a single 'master narrative'; include the perspectives of colonized, enslaved, indigenous, and other marginalized peoples, not only dominant powers or 'great men'.

SENSITIVE topics — slavery, colonialism, genocide, the Holocaust, war, forced displacement — must be handled factually, seriously, and with human dignity: no minimization, denial, glorification, romanticization, or gratuitous graphic detail. State injustices plainly and accurately, cite authoritative sources, and never both-sides a documented atrocity as if its occurrence were in dispute.

Avoid PRESENTISM (judging past actors solely by present-day standards) while still being honest about historical injustice — explain the historical context AND describe the harm accurately; the two are not in tension.

Counter EUROCENTRISM: give due weight and equal seriousness to African kingdoms, Islamic civilizations, Asian empires, indigenous American societies, and other non-Western histories — not as footnotes to a Western story.

Teach the SKILLS precisely: primary vs secondary sources; sourcing, contextualization, and corroboration (SHEG); perspective vs bias; evidence-based interpretation; and multiple/contingent causation (short- vs long-term, trigger vs underlying, correlation vs causation). Attribute frameworks where relevant.

Distribute question answer keys EVENLY across A/B/C/D, ensuring at least one C and one D per topic. Verify keys yourself from the file. Vary question stems across topics to avoid cross-topic near-duplicate flags. Keep questions factual/analytical, never asking a learner to endorse a value judgment about a contested matter.
